terms.definition: An AI system in which multiple agents coordinate, specialize, or hand work to one another to complete tasks that would otherwise be handled by a single agent.
terms.example: The research workflow used a multi-agent system with separate agents for retrieval, analysis, and review.

terms.definition: An AI capability that allows a model or agent to interact with a computer interface by interpreting the screen and taking actions such as moving a pointer, clicking, and typing.
terms.example: The agent used computer use to open a browser, navigate a website, and enter information into a form.

terms.definition: The coordination of models, agents, tools, prompts, data sources, and workflow steps so they operate together as one AI system or process.
terms.example: The orchestration layer routed the request to the right agent, tool, and retrieval source before returning the final answer.

terms.definition: A generative AI capability that creates images from natural-language descriptions or prompts.
terms.example: The designer used a text-to-image model to generate several concept illustrations from a written brief.

terms.definition: A sampling setting that influences how predictable or varied a model's generated output is by changing how strongly it favors higher-probability next tokens.
terms.example: Lowering the temperature made the model's responses more consistent, while a higher setting produced more varied wording.

terms.definition: A neural-network architecture that contains multiple expert subnetworks and uses a routing or gating mechanism to activate only some of them for a given input.
terms.example: The mixture-of-experts model routed each token to a small subset of its available expert networks.

terms.definition: A standardized task, dataset, or test suite used to compare the performance of AI models or systems under defined conditions.
terms.example: The team used a coding benchmark to compare how several models handled the same software-engineering tasks.

terms.definition: A structured evaluation used to measure whether an AI model or system meets specified performance, quality, safety, or reliability criteria.
terms.example: The team added an eval that checks whether the assistant cites the correct source before releasing a prompt change.

terms.definition: An evaluation method that uses a language model to score, compare, classify, or critique outputs according to a rubric or other judging criteria.
terms.example: The benchmark used LLM-as-a-judge for preliminary scoring, then compared the automated grades with human review.

terms.definition: Adversarial testing in which people or systems deliberately probe an AI system for harmful capabilities, weaknesses, unsafe behavior, or ways to bypass its safeguards.
terms.example: External red teaming found several jailbreak paths that the development team addressed before release.

terms.definition: The effort to make AI systems behave in ways that reliably follow intended human goals, values, instructions, and constraints.
terms.example: The alignment work focused on keeping the agent's actions consistent with user intent even during long, multi-step tasks.

terms.definition: A technical, policy, or workflow control designed to constrain AI behavior, reduce harmful outputs, or prevent unsafe actions.
terms.example: The application added a guardrail that blocks the agent from sending external messages without user approval.

terms.definition: A prompting attack intended to bypass an AI model's restrictions or refusal behavior so it produces content or actions the system is designed to prevent.
terms.example: The security test used a jailbreak attempt to see whether the model could be persuaded to ignore its safety restrictions.

terms.definition: The policies, roles, processes, controls, and oversight structures used to direct how an organization develops, acquires, deploys, monitors, and manages AI systems and their risks.
terms.example: The company created an AI governance process that defines approval, inventory, risk review, monitoring, and accountability for AI systems.

terms.definition: AI-generated or AI-manipulated image, audio, or video that realistically imitates a person, object, place, or event in a way that can falsely appear authentic.
terms.example: The fabricated video was identified as a deepfake after analysts found that the speaker's face and voice had been synthetically generated.

multi-agent-system.origin: Multi-agent systems predate generative AI and have long been studied in distributed artificial intelligence. In the current agentic-AI era, the term commonly describes workflows in which multiple coordinated AI agents divide work or hand tasks to one another.

history.event: OpenAI's practical guide to building agents described multi-agent systems as workflows distributed across multiple coordinated agents, including manager and decentralized handoff patterns.

sources.title: A practical guide to building AI agents

computer-use.origin: Computer use became a prominent AI capability label in 2024 as frontier models began interacting directly with graphical computer interfaces by interpreting screens and controlling pointers and keyboards.

firstKnownUse.note: Anthropic publicly introduced 'computer use' as a model capability in public beta on this date; AILex does not claim this was the first research on GUI automation.

history.event: Anthropic introduced computer use in public beta for Claude 3.5 Sonnet, describing screen viewing, cursor movement, clicking, and typing.

sources.title: Introducing computer use, a new Claude 3.5 Sonnet, and Claude 3.5 Haiku

orchestration.origin: Orchestration is an older computing term used for coordinating components and services. In AI systems it has been adapted to describe coordination among models, agents, tools, data sources, and workflow steps.

history.event: OpenAI's agent-building guidance described orchestration patterns for single-agent and multi-agent systems, including runs, loops, tool calls, and handoffs.

sources.title: A practical guide to building AI agents

text-to-image.origin: Text-to-image generation developed from research connecting natural-language representations with generative image models. The category entered broad public awareness as systems such as DALL·E demonstrated image creation from text prompts.

history.event: OpenAI introduced DALL·E, a neural network that creates images from text captions.

temperature.origin: Temperature comes from probabilistic sampling methods and predates modern generative AI. In language-model APIs it became a common user-facing control for adjusting randomness in token sampling.

sources.title: Create a model response - API Reference

mixture-of-experts.origin: Mixture-of-experts architectures grew from earlier neural-network research on combining specialized expert models with a gating mechanism. The approach became especially important for large-scale language models because sparse routing can increase model capacity without activating every parameter for every input.

history.event: Google researchers introduced a sparsely gated Mixture-of-Experts layer with up to thousands of expert subnetworks for language modeling and machine translation.

sources.title: Outrageously Large Neural Networks: The Sparsely-Gated Mixture-of-Experts Layer

benchmark.origin: Benchmark is an established evaluation term that predates modern AI. In machine learning and generative AI, benchmarks provide standardized tasks, datasets, or scoring procedures for comparing systems.

history.event: OpenAI and the SWE-bench authors released SWE-bench Verified, a human-validated subset for evaluating software-engineering performance.

eval.origin: Eval is a shortened form of evaluation that became common in modern AI development as teams formalized repeatable tests for model and system behavior. It can refer to a single test, a dataset-plus-grader configuration, or a broader evaluation suite.

history.event: OpenAI open-sourced Evals alongside GPT-4 as a framework for creating and running model benchmarks and inspecting performance sample by sample.
OpenAI described evals as methods to measure and improve whether an AI system meets expectations.

sources.title: How evals drive the next chapter in AI for businesses

llm-as-a-judge.origin: LLM-as-a-judge emerged as language models became capable enough to grade or compare other model outputs using natural-language rubrics. The broader idea overlaps with model-graded evaluation and automated grading.

history.event: OpenAI's GPT-4 release described 'model-graded evals,' noting that GPT-4 could check its own work.
OpenAI's PaperBench used an LLM-based judge to grade research-replication attempts against detailed rubrics and separately evaluated the judge itself.

red-teaming.origin: Red teaming is an established security practice that predates AI. AI red teaming adapts adversarial testing to probe models and systems for unsafe capabilities, failure modes, misuse pathways, and weaknesses in mitigations.

history.event: OpenAI's GPT-4o System Card documented large-scale external red teaming across safety, misuse, bias, privacy, impersonation, and other risk areas.

ai-alignment.origin: AI alignment is a research and safety term for the problem of making AI systems reliably pursue intended human goals and follow human values or intent. The underlying problem predates the current generative-AI era and has multiple competing formulations.

history.event: OpenAI described alignment research as work aimed at making AGI aligned with human values and human intent.
OpenAI described long-horizon alignment as requiring monitoring, safeguards, and iterative deployment because persistent models create new opportunities for unwanted actions.

sources.title: Safety and alignment in an era of long-horizon models

guardrail.origin: Guardrail is a general safety metaphor adapted to AI for controls that constrain behavior or reduce risk. AI guardrails can exist at model, system, policy, workflow, monitoring, or access-control layers rather than referring to one specific technique.

history.event: NIST reported that fixed AI guardrails cannot be universally robust against adaptive adversarial prompts, reinforcing the need for continuous monitoring and updating.

sources.title: NIST Mathematical Proof Supports Transition to a Continuous-Monitor-and-Update Security Model for AI Systems

jailbreak.origin: Jailbreak is an older computing term adapted to generative AI for prompts designed to bypass model restrictions or refusal behavior. It became common security vocabulary as public chatbots and safety controls proliferated.

history.event: NIST's adversarial machine-learning terminology defined jailbreak as a direct prompting attack intended to circumvent restrictions on model outputs.

ai-governance.origin: AI governance extends organizational governance and risk-management practices to AI systems. It covers the structures, policies, responsibilities, controls, documentation, oversight, and lifecycle processes used to direct AI development and use.

history.event: NIST released AI RMF 1.0 with GOVERN as a cross-cutting function covering policies, accountability, risk culture, roles, monitoring, inventories, and lifecycle oversight.

deepfake.origin: Deepfake emerged in the late 2010s as a popular label for highly realistic synthetic or manipulated media produced with deep-learning techniques. The term is now also used in law and policy for AI-generated or manipulated media that can falsely appear authentic.

history.event: The European Union AI Act defined 'deep fake' as AI-generated or manipulated image, audio, or video content that resembles real persons, objects, places, entities, or events and can falsely appear authentic or truthful.
